messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amina is a 20-year-old African woman who has been working as a pharmacist while trying to keep up with her relationship and her family’s expectations, but she now moves through her days as if the world has become a place of hidden ambushes. Her difficulties began after she was held and tortured during a period of political unrest, when she was forced to lie on the ground and had her body controlled against her will while she believed she might not survive. She does not tell the story easily; when she tries, the account fragments into pieces, and she says she can only remember flashes of hands, pressure, pain, and the hard surface beneath her. What remains most vividly is bodily: when the memory comes, she feels as though her own body is back in that position, pinned and helpless, while the rest stays incomplete and missing, almost impossible to put into words.

Since then, certain moments have become especially potent. Water, flooding, and large bodies of water unsettle her immediately, and so do arguments or any situation in which she feels forced to do something. A loud disagreement near her apartment building, a sink running too long, or seeing floodwater pooling in the street can bring back the same helpless bodily sensation and a rush of alarm. In those moments she becomes convinced that she must always be on guard, that she cannot afford to let her attention drift, and she thinks that if she even begins to remember the event in full she will not be able to handle it. She also feels guilty for surviving when others did not, and at times tells herself she deserves to suffer because of what happened. The combination leaves her feeling both frightened and morally condemned, as though danger and punishment are somehow still waiting for her.

That belief has shaped the way Amina moves through everyday life. She constantly scans her surroundings for signs of danger and identifies escape routes before she feels comfortable anywhere, whether she is entering the pharmacy where she works, sitting in a café with her partner, or arriving at a new building. If she is scheduled to close the pharmacy, she checks the back exit and the route to the parking lot before she can settle at the counter. At night she has difficulty falling asleep because she needs to stay alert, and she arranges her evening around avoiding the kinds of hours or situations that bring on nightmares. She also avoids seeing people who were involved in the event or who look similar to them, and even brief encounters with strangers who resemble those men can leave her tense and searching for a way out. These habits have narrowed her world, but she experiences them as necessary precautions rather than choices.

The more Amina tries to keep herself safe, the more the memory stays active. Scanning every room and mapping exits keeps her body braced in the same frozen posture, and the effort of staying alert makes the fragments of the torture return in sharper bodily form. Avoiding anything that might bring on dreams has not erased them; it has made sleep feel like another dangerous threshold, so that nights are organized around fear rather than rest. Her vigilance also feeds the very triggers she dreads, because arguments feel more explosive when she is already keyed up, and any sense of being cornered or forced intensifies her reactions. She has become more certain that she must be on guard all the time, and that certainty has deepened her conviction that she will not be able to bear what comes back to mind.

Over time, Amina has come to believe that thinking about the event itself is unsafe, so she pushes the memories away and treats them as if they were intolerable. Yet the more she avoids them, the less complete they feel, and the gaps in the story trouble her further; she is left with a disjointed bodily recollection that seems to prove something terrible happened, even if she cannot set it into words. The unfinished quality of the memory makes her more watchful, more ashamed, and more likely to interpret every argument, every sudden demand, every body of water, and every face that resembles her captors as a warning. That cycle has made her increasingly isolated at work and at home, and it was the growing impact on her sleep, her concentration at the pharmacy, and her relationship that finally brought her to seek help. What Amina says she wants most is to sleep without bracing for danger, but what frightens her most is that if she stops monitoring everything, the torture will return in full and she will not survive it a second time.
